content: 1. Zidovudine, a component of COMBIVIR, has been linked to hematologic toxicity, including neutropenia and anemia, particularly in patients with advanced HIV-1 disease. Regular blood count monitoring is strongly recommended for these patients. For other HIV-1-infected patients, periodic blood counts are advised. If anemia or neutropenia develops, dosage interruption may be necessary. 2. Myopathy and myositis, with pathological changes similar to those caused by HIV-1 disease, have been associated with prolonged use of zidovudine. These conditions may also occur during therapy with COMBIVIR. 3. Lactic acidosis and hepatomegaly with steatosis, including fatal cases, have been reported with the use of nucleoside analogues such as lamivudine and zidovudine, either alone or in combination with other antiretrovirals. These events have been more commonly reported in women, and risk factors may include obesity and prolonged nucleoside exposure. Caution is advised when administering COMBIVIR to patients with known risk factors for liver disease, although cases have also been reported in patients without such risk factors. Treatment with COMBIVIR should be discontinued in any patient who develops clinical or laboratory findings suggestive of lactic acidosis or significant hepatotoxicity, including hepatomegaly and steatosis, even in the absence of marked transaminase elevations. 4. In patients co-infected with HIV-1 and hepatitis B virus (HBV), discontinuation of lamivudine has been associated with exacerbations of hepatitis. These exacerbations, primarily detected by serum ALT elevations and re-emergence of HBV DNA, have been reported in clinical trials and post-marketing experience. While most events appear self-limited, fatalities have occurred in some cases. Patients should be closely monitored with clinical and laboratory follow-up for several months after stopping treatment. The impact of re-initiating lamivudine on post-treatment hepatitis exacerbations is unclear. 5. COMBIVIR contains a higher dose of lamivudine than EPIVIR-HBV, which is specifically developed for chronic hepatitis B treatment. The safety and efficacy of lamivudine for treating chronic hepatitis B in patients co-infected with HIV-1 and HBV have not been established. 6. Lamivudine-resistant HBV has been observed in non-HIV-infected patients treated with lamivudine for chronic hepatitis B, leading to diminished treatment response. Similar resistance has been reported in HIV-1-infected patients co-infected with HBV who received lamivudine-containing antiretroviral regimens. 7. COMBIVIR should not be used concurrently with other products containing lamivudine, zidovudine, or emtricitabine, such as EPIVIR, EPIVIR-HBV, RETROVIR, EPZICOM, TRIZIVIR, EMTRIVA, ATRIPLA, or TRUVADA. 8. Ribavirin has been shown in vitro to reduce the phosphorylation of lamivudine and zidovudine. Co-administration of ribavirin with lamivudine or zidovudine in HIV-1/HCV co-infected patients has been associated with loss of virologic suppression and hepatic decompensation, some of which were fatal. Patients receiving interferon alfa with or without ribavirin and COMBIVIR should be closely monitored for toxicities, including hepatic decompensation, neutropenia, and anemia. Co-administration of ribavirin and zidovudine is not recommended due to the risk of exacerbating anemia. 9. COMBIVIR should be used cautiously in patients with a history of pancreatitis or other significant risk factors for pancreatitis. Treatment should be discontinued immediately if clinical signs, symptoms, or laboratory abnormalities suggestive of pancreatitis occur. 10. Immune reconstitution syndrome has been reported in patients treated with combination antiretroviral therapy, including COMBIVIR. During the initial phase of treatment, patients with improving immune systems may develop an inflammatory response to residual or indolent opportunistic infections, such as Mycobacterium avium, cytomegalovirus, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, or tuberculosis, requiring further evaluation and treatment. 11. Redistribution or accumulation of body fat, including central obesity, dorsocervical fat enlargement (buffalo hump), peripheral wasting, facial wasting, breast enlargement, and a cushingoid appearance, has been observed in patients receiving antiretroviral therapy. The mechanism and long-term consequences of these events are not fully understood, and a causal relationship has not been established.
